blocks.text: GOVT. T. ROMANA COLLEGE NOTES
VALUE ADDED COURSE (VAC)
BATCH 3 — VAC 103
ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE
WHOLE SYLLABUS • SHORT NOTES & LONG NOTES
2 Credits | Full Marks: 75+25 | For use by students of Govt. T. Romana College only.
If you are not taking VAC 103 – Environmental Science, there is no need to study this section.
This is a universal VAC paper. Scientific terms are explained in simple college-level English so that students from Arts and other backgrounds can understand them.
The official syllabus has two units. Unit I deals with Environmental Science, natural resources, ecosystems and biodiversity. Unit II deals with pollution and solid-waste management.
For short answers, learn the definition, causes or components, effects and control/conservation points. For long answers, explain the concept systematically with examples.
These notes are organised strictly around the topics listed in the prescribed VAC 103 syllabus.

sections.title: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY

sections.title: Environmental Science
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Environmental Science is the systematic study of the environment and the interaction of its physical, chemical, biological and human components. It examines environmental problems and ways of protecting natural systems.

The word 'environment' comes from the French word 'environner', meaning 'to surround'. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, defines environment to include 'water, air and land and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land, and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property'.

The environment has four main segments: the atmosphere (air), the hydrosphere (water), the lithosphere (land and soil) and the biosphere (the zone where life exists). Environmental Science studies all of these and how human activities affect them.

sections.title: Scope of Environmental Science
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Its scope includes natural resources, ecosystems, biodiversity, pollution, conservation, waste management and human interaction with the environment.

The scope of Environmental Science also covers climate change, ozone depletion, disaster management, environmental laws and policies, environmental impact assessment (EIA), environmental ethics, sustainable development and environmental education.

It also provides career opportunities in research, environmental consultancy, pollution control boards, forestry, wildlife conservation, NGOs, environmental journalism and waste management industries.

sections.title: Importance of Environmental Science
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: It helps us understand environmental problems, conserve resources, protect biodiversity, reduce pollution and make informed decisions for sustainable living.

Environmental Science helps people understand problems such as global warming, deforestation, pollution and loss of biodiversity, and encourages responsible behaviour. It is important for sustainable development, which the Brundtland Report (1987) defined as 'development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'.

In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1991), the Supreme Court of India directed that environmental education be taught as a compulsory subject at all levels of education. This is one reason why Environmental Science is included in college courses.

sections.title: Multidisciplinary Nature
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Environmental Science is multidisciplinary because environmental problems require knowledge from biology, chemistry, physics, geology, geography, economics, sociology, law, public policy and other fields.

Environmental Science draws on many subjects: biology (ecology, biodiversity), chemistry (pollutants and their reactions), physics (energy, radiation, noise), geology and geography (land, soil, water resources), mathematics and statistics (data analysis), economics (the cost of pollution and resource use), sociology (human behaviour and communities), law (environmental legislation) and engineering (pollution control technology).
Because environmental problems are complex, solving them requires cooperation between scientists, engineers, economists, lawyers, policymakers and citizens.

sections.title: Natural Resources
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Natural resources are useful materials and conditions obtained from nature, such as water, soil, forests, minerals, sunlight and biological resources.
Natural resources are materials and energy sources found in nature that are useful to human beings, such as air, water, soil, forests, minerals, fossil fuels, sunlight and wildlife.
The main types of natural resources studied in Environmental Science include forest resources, water resources, mineral resources, food resources, energy resources and land resources.

sections.title: Classification of Natural Resources
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Resources may be classified in different ways. A common distinction is renewable resources, which can be naturally replenished, and non-renewable resources, which form very slowly and can be exhausted.

Natural resources can be classified on the basis of origin into biotic resources (obtained from living things, such as forests, animals and fish) and abiotic resources (obtained from non-living things, such as water, air, minerals and land).

On the basis of renewability, they are classified as renewable (such as solar energy, wind, water, forests) and non-renewable (such as coal, petroleum, natural gas and minerals). Some writers also mention inexhaustible resources such as sunlight and wind.
On the basis of development, resources may be potential (known but not yet used), actual (being used) or reserve (known but kept for future use).

sections.title: Renewable Resources
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Renewable resources can regenerate naturally within a useful time when properly managed. Examples include solar energy, wind, water and biological resources.

Renewable resources can be replenished naturally within a reasonable time, but only if they are used carefully. For example, forests can regrow if trees are not cut faster than they grow, and groundwater can be recharged if it is not overdrawn.

Renewable energy sources include solar, wind, hydroelectric, biomass, geothermal and tidal energy. India has set targets to increase its use of non-fossil fuel energy capacity under its climate commitments.

sections.title: Non-renewable Resources
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Non-renewable resources exist in limited stocks or form over very long geological periods. Coal, petroleum and many mineral deposits are examples.

Non-renewable resources take millions of years to form and are available only in limited quantities. Fossil fuels (coal, petroleum and natural gas) were formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas responsible for global warming. Minerals such as iron, copper and aluminium are also non-renewable, though they can be recycled.

sections.title: Depletion of Natural Resources
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Resource depletion means reduction in the quantity or quality of natural resources because use exceeds renewal or because resources are damaged.

Depletion of natural resources means using them faster than they can be replaced. Examples include deforestation, overfishing, depletion of groundwater, soil erosion and exhaustion of mineral reserves.

The Global Footprint Network calculates 'Earth Overshoot Day', the date each year by which humanity has used more resources than the Earth can regenerate in that year. In recent years this date has fallen in late July or early August.

sections.title: Causes of Resource Depletion
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Major causes include overconsumption, deforestation, mining, pollution, population pressure, unsustainable extraction and inefficient use.

The main causes of resource depletion are population growth, overconsumption, industrialization, urbanization, deforestation for agriculture and development projects, pollution, wasteful use, poverty (which forces people to depend heavily on natural resources) and poor management.

In north-eastern India, including Mizoram, shortening jhum (shifting cultivation) cycles have contributed to soil erosion and forest degradation, because land is not given enough time to recover between cultivation periods.

sections.title: Conservation of Natural Resources
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Conservation means planned protection and wise use of resources so that they remain available and ecological systems are not unnecessarily damaged.

Conservation means the wise use of natural resources so that they last longer and benefit both present and future generations. The 3Rs — Reduce, Reuse and Recycle — are basic principles of conservation.

Methods include afforestation and reforestation, rainwater harvesting, watershed management, soil conservation through terracing and contour farming, use of renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable agriculture, protected areas for wildlife, and community participation such as the Chipko movement and Joint Forest Management.
In Mizoram, programmes promoting settled cultivation, horticulture and village forest reserves (commonly known as village safety reserves and supply reserves) help conserve land and forest resources.

sections.title: Ecosystem
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: An ecosystem is a functional unit in which living organisms interact with one another and with non-living components such as air, water, soil and sunlight.

The term 'ecosystem' was coined by the British ecologist A.G. Tansley in 1935. E.P. Odum defined it as the basic functional unit of ecology, including both living organisms and their non-living environment, each influencing the properties of the other.
Ecosystems vary in size from a small pond or a rotting log to a large forest or an ocean. The largest ecosystem is the biosphere.

sections.title: Biotic Components
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Biotic components are the living parts of an ecosystem, including producers, consumers and decomposers.
Biotic components are the living parts of an ecosystem. They are divided into producers (autotrophs), consumers (heterotrophs) and decomposers (saprotrophs).

Biotic components interact with each other through relationships such as predation, competition, parasitism, mutualism (both benefit, such as bees and flowers) and commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected).

sections.title: Abiotic Components
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Abiotic components are non-living environmental factors such as sunlight, temperature, water, air, soil and minerals.

Abiotic components are the non-living parts of an ecosystem. They include climatic factors (sunlight, temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind), edaphic or soil factors (soil type, minerals, pH), and inorganic and organic substances (water, carbon dioxide, oxygen, nitrogen, proteins and carbohydrates in dead matter).
Abiotic factors determine which organisms can live in a particular place. For example, the high rainfall and warm temperatures of Mizoram support dense tropical and subtropical forests.

sections.title: Producers
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Producers, mainly green plants and algae, manufacture organic food using energy, usually through photosynthesis.
Producers are organisms that make their own food through photosynthesis, using sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and oxygen. Green plants, algae and some bacteria are producers.
Producers form the first trophic level and are the base of all food chains. Without them, no other organism could survive.

sections.title: Consumers
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Consumers obtain energy by eating plants or other organisms. Herbivores, carnivores and omnivores are common consumer groups.

Consumers depend on other organisms for food. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat plants, such as deer, cattle and grasshoppers. Secondary consumers (carnivores) eat herbivores, such as frogs and snakes. Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers, such as eagles and tigers.
Omnivores, such as human beings and bears, eat both plants and animals.

sections.title: Decomposers
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Decomposers such as many bacteria and fungi break down dead organic matter and help return nutrients to the environment.
Decomposers are microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi that break down dead plants, animals and waste into simpler substances, returning nutrients to the soil.

Decomposers are essential for nutrient cycling. Without them, dead matter would pile up and nutrients would not be available for producers. Earthworms and some insects, called detritivores, also help in this process.

sections.title: Structure of an Ecosystem
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Ecosystem structure refers to its biotic and abiotic components and their organisation, including trophic levels and feeding relationships.

The structure of an ecosystem includes its species composition, the arrangement of trophic levels, the distribution of biomass and energy, and its stratification (vertical layers, as in a forest with canopy, understorey, shrub and ground layers).

Ecological pyramids show the structure of an ecosystem. The pyramid of numbers shows the number of organisms at each level, the pyramid of biomass shows the weight of living matter, and the pyramid of energy shows the energy at each level. The pyramid of energy is always upright.

sections.title: Functions of an Ecosystem
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Important ecosystem functions include energy flow, nutrient cycling, production of biomass, decomposition and regulation of ecological interactions.

The main functions of an ecosystem are energy flow, nutrient (biogeochemical) cycling, productivity and regulation. Energy flows in one direction from the sun to producers to consumers and is lost as heat at each level.
R.L. Lindeman's ten per cent law (1942) states that only about 10 per cent of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next. This is why food chains usually have only four or five levels.

Nutrients move in cycles, such as the carbon, nitrogen, water and phosphorus cycles. Ecosystems also provide services such as clean air, clean water, pollination, soil formation and climate regulation.

sections.title: Food Chain
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: A food chain shows a simple sequence through which food and energy pass from one organism to another.
A food chain is the sequence of organisms through which energy and nutrients pass, each being eaten by the next. Example: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.
There are two main types: the grazing food chain, which starts with green plants, and the detritus food chain, which starts with dead organic matter.

sections.title: Food Web
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: A food web is a network of interconnected food chains and better represents the multiple feeding relationships in a real ecosystem.
A food web is a network of interconnected food chains in an ecosystem. Most organisms eat more than one kind of food and are eaten by more than one kind of predator.
Food webs make ecosystems more stable, because if one food source declines, consumers can switch to another. A complex food web indicates a healthy ecosystem.

sections.title: Terrestrial Ecosystem
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: A terrestrial ecosystem occurs on land. Forests, grasslands and deserts are examples.
Terrestrial ecosystems are land-based ecosystems, including forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra. India has tropical evergreen, tropical deciduous, montane, thorn and mangrove forests.

Forest ecosystems are important for oxygen production, carbon storage, rainfall regulation, soil conservation and biodiversity. According to the India State of Forest Report, Mizoram has one of the highest proportions of forest cover among Indian states, at over 80 per cent of its geographical area.

sections.title: Aquatic Ecosystem
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: An aquatic ecosystem occurs in water and includes freshwater and marine systems such as ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans.

Aquatic ecosystems are water-based and include freshwater ecosystems (ponds, lakes, rivers, wetlands) and marine ecosystems (oceans, seas, coral reefs, estuaries). Estuaries, where rivers meet the sea, are among the most productive ecosystems.

Important organisms in aquatic ecosystems include phytoplankton (producers), zooplankton, fish and decomposers. Palak Dil in southern Mizoram is the largest natural lake in the state. Wetlands are protected internationally under the Ramsar Convention (1971).

sections.title: Artificial Ecosystem
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: An artificial ecosystem is created or strongly managed by humans, such as a crop field, garden, reservoir or aquarium.
Artificial or man-made ecosystems are created and maintained by human beings, such as croplands, gardens, aquariums, parks, dams and urban areas.

They usually have low biodiversity and depend on human inputs such as fertilizers, water and energy. Agricultural ecosystems, for example, often grow a single crop (monoculture), which makes them vulnerable to pests.

sections.title: Ecological Succession
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Ecological succession is the gradual change in the species composition and structure of a biological community over time.

Ecological succession is the gradual and orderly process by which one community of organisms is replaced by another in an area over time, until a stable climax community is formed. F.E. Clements was an important early theorist of succession.
The first organisms to colonize an area are called pioneer species, the intermediate communities are called seral stages, and the final stable community is called the climax community.

sections.title: Primary Succession
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Primary succession begins on a surface where a developed biological community and soil are initially absent, such as newly exposed rock.

Primary succession occurs in an area where no life existed before, such as bare rock, a new volcanic island or a newly formed sand dune. Lichens and mosses are typical pioneer species on rocks; they break down the rock and help form soil.

Succession that begins on bare rock is called a xerosere or lithosere, while succession that begins in water, such as a pond, is called a hydrosere. Primary succession takes a very long time, often hundreds or thousands of years.

sections.title: Secondary Succession
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Secondary succession occurs where a previous community has been disturbed but soil or other biological legacies remain.

Secondary succession occurs in an area where a community existed but was destroyed by disturbance, such as fire, flood, deforestation or abandoned farmland. Because soil is already present, secondary succession is faster than primary succession.
Abandoned jhum fields in Mizoram are an example: grasses and shrubs appear first, followed by bamboo and secondary forest. If the land is left long enough, a more mature forest can develop.

sections.title: Biodiversity
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Biodiversity means the variety of living organisms and ecological variation. It can be studied at genetic, species and ecosystem levels.

The term 'biodiversity' (a short form of biological diversity) was used by Walter G. Rosen in 1985 and popularized by the American biologist E.O. Wilson. The Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), adopted at the Rio Earth Summit, defines it as the variability among living organisms from all sources and the ecological complexes of which they are a part.
India is one of the world's 17 megadiverse countries. It has only about 2.4 per cent of the world's land area but accounts for about 7-8 per cent of recorded species.

sections.title: Genetic Diversity
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Genetic diversity is variation in genes within a species or population. It helps populations adapt to environmental change.
Genetic diversity is the variation of genes within a species. It allows populations to adapt to changes in the environment and resist diseases.
Examples include the many varieties of rice grown in India and the different breeds of cattle. Loss of genetic diversity makes species more vulnerable to extinction.

sections.title: Species Diversity
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Species diversity refers to the variety and relative abundance of different species in an area.

Species diversity refers to the variety of species in a particular area. It includes species richness (the number of species) and species evenness (how evenly individuals are distributed among species).
Tropical rainforests have the highest species diversity on land, while coral reefs have very high diversity in the sea.

sections.title: Ecosystem Diversity
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Ecosystem diversity refers to the variety of habitats, ecological communities and ecosystems in a region.
Ecosystem diversity is the variety of ecosystems in a region, such as forests, grasslands, wetlands, rivers, deserts and mountains.
India has great ecosystem diversity, from the Himalayan mountains to the Thar Desert, the Western Ghats, the Sundarbans mangroves, coral reefs and the forests of the North-East.

sections.title: Biodiversity Hotspot
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: A biodiversity hotspot is a region with exceptionally high concentrations of endemic species that has also experienced severe habitat loss and is therefore a major conservation priority.

The concept of biodiversity hotspots was introduced by the British ecologist Norman Myers in 1988. According to Conservation International, a region qualifies as a hotspot if it has at least 1,500 species of endemic vascular plants and has lost at least 70 per cent of its original natural vegetation.

There are 36 recognized biodiversity hotspots in the world. Four of them include parts of India: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (which includes the Nicobar Islands).

sections.title: Biodiversity Hotspots and Northeast India
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Northeast India is especially important because it lies within the Indo-Burma biodiversity hotspot, while parts of the wider northeastern region are also associated with the Himalaya hotspot.

The Indo-Burma hotspot includes most of North-East India (south of the Brahmaputra river), Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam and southern China. It is rich in endemic plants, freshwater fish, turtles and birds.

Mizoram's protected areas include the Dampa Tiger Reserve, Murlen National Park and Phawngpui (Blue Mountain) National Park. Species found in the region include the hoolock gibbon (India's only ape), clouded leopard, Hume's pheasant (Mizoram's state bird) and many orchids.

sections.title: Causes of Biodiversity Loss
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Major causes include habitat destruction and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution, climate change and other human pressures.

The main causes of biodiversity loss are often remembered by the acronym HIPPO: Habitat destruction, Invasive species, Pollution, Population growth (human) and Overexploitation (hunting, overfishing, illegal wildlife trade). Climate change is now another major cause.

In the North-East, hunting, shifting cultivation with short cycles, logging, road construction and mining threaten biodiversity. The flowering of bamboo (mautam) in Mizoram, which occurs about every 48 years, leads to rat population explosions that damage crops and can cause famine.

sections.title: Effects of Biodiversity Loss
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Biodiversity loss can weaken ecosystem stability and services, reduce genetic resources, disrupt food webs and cause irreversible extinction of species.
Biodiversity loss reduces ecosystem services such as pollination, water purification, soil fertility and climate regulation. It also reduces the availability of food, medicine and raw materials.
Loss of biodiversity can make ecosystems less resilient to disasters and diseases and can harm the livelihoods and cultures of people who depend on forests and rivers, especially tribal communities.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY

sections.title: Environmental Science: Scope, Importance and Multidisciplinary Nature
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Environmental Science studies the environment and the relationships among living organisms, physical surroundings and human activities. It is concerned both with understanding natural systems and with solving environmental problems.

Its scope includes natural resources, ecosystems, biodiversity, pollution, conservation and waste management. Environmental issues are connected with health, economy, society and government, so they cannot be understood through one subject alone.

Environmental Science is therefore multidisciplinary. Biology helps explain organisms and ecosystems; chemistry explains pollutants and chemical cycles; geology and geography help explain land and resources; economics and social sciences help us understand consumption, development and human behaviour. This broad approach makes Environmental Science important for responsible and sustainable decision-making.

Environmental Science is the study of the environment and the interactions between its physical, chemical, biological and human components. It covers the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere.
Its scope includes natural resources, ecosystems, biodiversity, pollution, waste management, climate change, environmental laws, environmental impact assessment and sustainable development.

Its importance lies in creating awareness, guiding sustainable development, helping solve environmental problems and supporting policies. The Supreme Court, in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1991), directed that environmental education be compulsory at all levels.

Environmental Science is multidisciplinary because it uses knowledge from biology, chemistry, physics, geography, economics, sociology, law and engineering. Environmental problems such as climate change cannot be solved by any single subject.
In conclusion, Environmental Science helps students understand their responsibility towards the environment and prepares them to participate in protecting it.

sections.title: Natural Resources: Concept, Classification, Depletion and Conservation
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Natural resources are materials, organisms and environmental conditions that people and ecosystems depend upon. Water, soil, forests, minerals, sunlight and fossil fuels are examples.

Resources can be classified in several ways. A useful distinction is between renewable resources, which can regenerate naturally, and non-renewable resources, which exist in limited stocks or require extremely long periods to form.

Resources become depleted when extraction or damage occurs faster than natural replacement. Deforestation, excessive mining, overuse of water, pollution, wasteful consumption and unsustainable development can cause depletion.

Conservation involves planned and responsible use. Important measures include reducing waste, recycling materials, protecting forests and water sources, improving efficiency and using renewable alternatives where suitable. Conservation does not always mean stopping use; it means using resources in a way that protects their long-term availability and ecological functions.
Natural resources are things found in nature that are useful to human beings. They are classified as biotic or abiotic, renewable or non-renewable, and potential, actual or reserve.

Renewable resources such as forests, water and solar energy can be replenished, but only if they are used sustainably. Non-renewable resources such as coal, petroleum and minerals are limited and take millions of years to form.

Depletion of resources is caused by population growth, overconsumption, industrialization, deforestation, pollution and poor management. Examples include falling groundwater levels, deforestation and soil erosion.

Conservation methods include the 3Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle), afforestation, rainwater harvesting, soil conservation, renewable energy, sustainable agriculture and community participation. Laws such as the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, support conservation.
In conclusion, sustainable use of natural resources is essential for the survival and well-being of present and future generations.

sections.title: Ecosystem: Components, Structure and Functions
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
An ecosystem is a functional unit formed by interactions between living organisms and their non-living environment. The non-living or abiotic components include sunlight, air, water, soil, temperature and minerals. The living or biotic components include producers, consumers and decomposers.

Producers capture energy and make organic matter. Consumers obtain energy by feeding on other organisms. Decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the environment.

The structure of an ecosystem includes these components, trophic levels and feeding relationships. Its major functions include energy flow, nutrient cycling, biological production and decomposition.

A food chain shows a simple feeding sequence, while a food web shows the many interconnected feeding relationships that actually occur. Ecosystem health depends on the continued interaction of its components rather than on any one species or factor alone.
An ecosystem, a term coined by A.G. Tansley in 1935, is a community of living organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living environment as a functional unit.
Its components are biotic (producers, consumers and decomposers) and abiotic (climatic factors, soil factors and inorganic and organic substances).
The structure of an ecosystem includes species composition, trophic levels and stratification, which can be shown through pyramids of numbers, biomass and energy.

The functions of an ecosystem include energy flow (following Lindeman's ten per cent law), nutrient cycling (carbon, nitrogen, water and phosphorus cycles), productivity and regulation. Food chains and food webs show how energy moves through the ecosystem.
In conclusion, ecosystems provide essential services such as clean air, water, food and climate regulation, and must be protected.

sections.title: Major Ecosystems: Terrestrial, Aquatic and Artificial
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Terrestrial ecosystems occur on land. Forests, grasslands and deserts are common examples. Their organisms and ecological processes are strongly influenced by climate, soil and availability of water.

Aquatic ecosystems occur in water. Freshwater systems include ponds, lakes and rivers, while marine ecosystems include seas and oceans. Water conditions, depth, light, salinity and nutrients influence aquatic life.

Artificial ecosystems are created or strongly managed by human beings. Crop fields, gardens, reservoirs and aquariums are examples. They may require continued human inputs and management.

The classification helps us understand that ecosystems differ in structure and species, but all involve interaction between biotic and abiotic components.

Terrestrial ecosystems include forests, grasslands, deserts and tundra. Forests are especially important for oxygen, carbon storage, biodiversity and soil and water conservation. India has tropical evergreen, deciduous, montane and mangrove forests.
Aquatic ecosystems include freshwater ecosystems (ponds, lakes, rivers, wetlands) and marine ecosystems (oceans, coral reefs, estuaries). They support fisheries, provide water and regulate climate.
Artificial ecosystems such as croplands, gardens, aquariums and cities are created by human beings and depend on human inputs. They are usually less diverse and less stable than natural ecosystems.
Examples from Mizoram include its dense hill forests (terrestrial), rivers such as the Tlawng and Tuirial and Palak Dil lake (aquatic), and terraced farms, orchards and urban Aizawl (artificial).
In conclusion, all ecosystems are connected, and human activities in one ecosystem can affect others.

sections.title: Ecological Succession
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Ecological succession is the gradual and directional change in the composition of a biological community over time. It may occur after a new surface becomes available or after an existing ecosystem is disturbed.

Primary succession begins where developed soil and an established biological community are initially absent. Pioneer organisms begin colonisation, and their activities gradually help create conditions for other organisms.

Secondary succession occurs after disturbance in an area where soil or biological material remains. Because some ecological foundations are already present, recovery is generally faster than in primary succession.

Succession demonstrates that ecosystems are dynamic. Their composition can change through colonisation, competition, environmental modification and disturbance.
Ecological succession is the gradual replacement of one community by another until a stable climax community is formed.

Primary succession occurs in areas without previous life, such as bare rock (xerosere) or water (hydrosere), starting with pioneer species such as lichens and mosses. Secondary succession occurs in areas where a community was disturbed, such as burned forests or abandoned farmland, and is faster because soil is already present.

The stages of succession are nudation (formation of a bare area), invasion (arrival of pioneer species), competition and coaction, reaction (modification of the environment by organisms), stabilization and the climax community.
Understanding succession is important for forest regeneration, restoration of degraded land and the management of shifting cultivation areas.
In conclusion, succession shows that ecosystems are dynamic and can recover over time if disturbances are reduced.

sections.title: Biodiversity: Meaning, Levels and Importance
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Biodiversity is the variety of life. It includes genetic diversity within species, species diversity within communities and ecosystem diversity across landscapes.

Genetic diversity helps populations adapt to changing conditions. Species diversity contributes to ecological interactions and ecosystem functioning. Ecosystem diversity provides a variety of habitats and ecological processes.

Biodiversity is important because human societies depend on functioning ecosystems for food, materials, medicines, pollination, soil processes, water regulation and many other benefits. It also has scientific, cultural and ecological value.

Conserving biodiversity therefore means protecting not only individual species but also genetic variation, habitats and ecological relationships.

Biodiversity means the variety of life on Earth at the genetic, species and ecosystem levels. The term was popularized by E.O. Wilson, and the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) provides the international framework for its conservation.
Genetic diversity is variation within a species, species diversity is the variety of species in an area, and ecosystem diversity is the variety of ecosystems in a region.

Biodiversity has many values: consumptive use value (food, fuel, medicine), productive use value (commercial products such as timber), social and cultural value, ethical value, aesthetic value and ecosystem service value.

India is a megadiverse country. Laws such as the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, protect biodiversity. Conservation methods include in-situ conservation (national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves) and ex-situ conservation (zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks).
In conclusion, biodiversity is essential for ecological balance and human well-being, and its conservation is a shared responsibility.

sections.title: Biodiversity Hotspots, Causes and Effects of Biodiversity Loss
context: UNIT I — ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCE AND BIODIVERSITY
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
A biodiversity hotspot is a region containing exceptionally high levels of endemic plant diversity that has also lost a very large proportion of its original natural vegetation. Hotspots are therefore priorities for conservation because they combine biological uniqueness with serious threat.

Northeast India is highly significant in biodiversity studies because it lies within the Indo-Burma hotspot, and parts of the broader northeastern region are associated with the Himalaya hotspot.

Biodiversity is lost through habitat destruction and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution, climate change and other pressures. Habitat loss is especially serious because species may lose food, breeding areas and ecological connections.

The effects include extinction, disruption of food webs, reduced genetic resources and weakening of ecosystem functions and services. Because extinction is irreversible, prevention and conservation are particularly important.

Norman Myers introduced the concept of biodiversity hotspots in 1988. There are 36 hotspots worldwide, and India includes parts of four: the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland.

North-East India, including Mizoram, is part of the Indo-Burma hotspot and has a rich variety of plants, orchids, birds, primates such as the hoolock gibbon, and other wildlife. Protected areas such as Dampa Tiger Reserve and Phawngpui National Park help conserve this biodiversity.

Causes of biodiversity loss include habitat destruction, invasive species, pollution, human population growth, overexploitation and climate change. In the North-East, hunting, logging, shortened jhum cycles and infrastructure development are additional pressures.

Effects include extinction of species, loss of ecosystem services, reduced food and medicinal resources and harm to communities dependent on forests. Conservation requires protected areas, community participation, sustainable livelihoods and awareness.
In conclusion, protecting hotspots is a global priority because they hold a large share of the Earth's unique species in a small area.

sections.title: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT

sections.title: Environmental Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Environmental pollution is an undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological quality of the environment that can harm organisms, ecosystems or human welfare.

Environmental pollution is defined as the undesirable change in the physical, chemical or biological characteristics of air, water or soil that may harm human beings, other living organisms and property.

Pollution can be natural, such as volcanic eruptions and forest fires, or caused by human activities, such as industry, transport and agriculture. Human-caused pollution is the main concern of environmental science.

sections.title: Pollutant
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: A pollutant is a substance or form of energy present at a harmful concentration or in an inappropriate place in the environment.

A pollutant is a substance or form of energy that causes pollution. Pollutants may be primary (released directly into the environment, such as carbon monoxide and sulphur dioxide) or secondary (formed by reactions in the environment, such as ground-level ozone and smog).
Pollutants can also be classified as biodegradable (broken down by natural processes, such as sewage) or non-biodegradable (not easily broken down, such as plastics, DDT and heavy metals).

sections.title: Sources of Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Pollution sources may include industries, vehicles, households, agriculture, construction, mining, energy production and improper waste disposal.
Sources of pollution may be point sources (a single identifiable source, such as a factory outlet pipe) or non-point sources (spread over a wide area, such as runoff from agricultural fields).
Major sources include industries, vehicles, thermal power plants, agriculture (fertilizers and pesticides), domestic waste, mining, construction and burning of waste and crop residue.

sections.title: Types of Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: The prescribed syllabus focuses on air, water, soil and noise pollution, along with solid-waste problems.

The main types of pollution are air, water, soil and noise pollution. Other types include thermal pollution (from hot water released by power plants), radioactive pollution, light pollution and marine pollution.

The main laws in India include the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The Central Pollution Control Board and State Pollution Control Boards enforce these laws.

sections.title: Air Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Air pollution occurs when harmful gases, particles or biological materials contaminate the atmosphere at levels capable of causing damage.
Air pollution is the presence of harmful substances in the atmosphere in quantities that harm human health, other living things or the environment.

Major air pollutants include particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), sulphur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx), carbon monoxide (CO), ground-level ozone (O3), ammonia and lead. India uses the National Air Quality Index (launched in 2014) to report air quality.

sections.title: Causes of Air Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Major causes include vehicle exhaust, fossil-fuel combustion, industries, open burning, construction dust and some natural events.

Causes of air pollution include vehicle exhaust, burning of fossil fuels in power plants and industries, construction dust, burning of crop residue (stubble burning), burning of waste, use of firewood and coal for cooking, and forest fires.
In hill states like Mizoram, burning of forests for jhum cultivation in the dry season (February to April) causes seasonal smoke and haze.

sections.title: Effects of Air Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Air pollution can cause respiratory and cardiovascular problems, reduce visibility, damage plants and materials and contribute to wider atmospheric problems.
Air pollution causes respiratory diseases such as asthma and bronchitis, heart disease, lung cancer and eye irritation. Fine particles (PM2.5) can enter deep into the lungs and bloodstream.

Environmental effects include acid rain (from SO2 and NOx), smog, damage to crops and forests, depletion of the ozone layer (by chlorofluorocarbons, controlled under the Montreal Protocol, 1987), and global warming (from greenhouse gases).
Historical disasters include the London smog of 1952 and the Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984, in which methyl isocyanate gas leaked from a pesticide plant, killing thousands of people.

sections.title: Control of Air Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Control measures include cleaner fuels and energy, emission standards, public transport, industrial pollution-control equipment, dust control and prevention of open burning.

Control methods include using cleaner fuels (CNG, LPG, electric vehicles), emission standards for vehicles (India adopted Bharat Stage VI norms from 1 April 2020), installing pollution control devices in industries (electrostatic precipitators, scrubbers, filters, catalytic converters), planting trees, and promoting public transport.
Policies include the National Clean Air Programme (2019), the Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (2016), which provides LPG connections to poor households, and bans on burning waste and crop residue.

sections.title: Water Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Water pollution is contamination that changes water quality and makes it harmful or less suitable for organisms and human use.
Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies such as rivers, lakes, oceans and groundwater by harmful substances, making the water unfit for use.

Water quality is measured using parameters such as biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), dissolved oxygen (DO), pH, turbidity and the presence of coliform bacteria. High BOD indicates heavy organic pollution.

sections.title: Causes of Water Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Untreated sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, oil, plastics and improper disposal of waste are major causes.

Causes include the discharge of untreated domestic sewage, industrial effluents containing chemicals and heavy metals, agricultural runoff with fertilizers and pesticides, oil spills, dumping of solid waste and plastics, and mining.
Religious and cultural practices such as immersing idols painted with toxic colours have also contributed to river pollution in some areas.

sections.title: Effects of Water Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: It can spread disease, reduce dissolved oxygen, kill aquatic organisms, contaminate food chains and make water unsafe.

Water pollution causes waterborne diseases such as cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea, dysentery and hepatitis. Heavy metals cause serious illnesses, for example Minamata disease (mercury poisoning) in Japan and itai-itai disease (cadmium poisoning).

Excess nutrients from fertilizers and sewage cause eutrophication, which leads to algal blooms, oxygen depletion and the death of fish. Biomagnification means that toxic substances such as DDT and mercury become more concentrated at higher levels of the food chain.

sections.title: Control of Water Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Control requires sewage and effluent treatment, protection of water bodies, reduced dumping, careful agricultural chemical use and monitoring of water quality.

Control measures include treating sewage in sewage treatment plants, treating industrial effluents before discharge, reducing the use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides, banning dumping of waste into rivers, and protecting watersheds and wetlands.

Programmes include the Ganga Action Plan (launched in 1986), Namami Gange (2014), the National River Conservation Plan and the Jal Jeevan Mission (2019), which aims to provide safe tap water to rural households.

sections.title: Soil Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Soil pollution is contamination or degradation of soil by harmful chemicals, wastes or other pollutants.
Soil pollution is the presence of toxic chemicals or other harmful materials in the soil at levels that are harmful to plants, animals and human beings.
Pollutants in soil include pesticides, excess fertilizers, heavy metals (lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury), plastics, industrial waste and e-waste.

sections.title: Causes of Soil Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Excessive pesticides and fertilisers, industrial waste, mining, oil leakage, plastics and improper dumping can pollute soil.

Causes include excessive use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides, dumping of industrial and municipal solid waste, mining, leakage from landfills, improper disposal of e-waste and plastics, and acid rain.
Deforestation and soil erosion also degrade soil quality by removing fertile topsoil.

sections.title: Effects of Soil Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: It can reduce soil fertility, harm soil organisms, contaminate crops and groundwater and introduce toxic substances into food chains.
Soil pollution reduces soil fertility and crop yields, harms soil organisms such as earthworms and microbes, and allows toxic substances to enter the food chain.

Polluted soil can contaminate groundwater and cause health problems such as cancer, kidney damage and nervous system disorders. Arsenic contamination of groundwater and soil is a serious problem in parts of West Bengal and Bihar.

sections.title: Control of Soil Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Control measures include responsible chemical use, safe waste disposal, recycling, treatment of contaminated sites and sustainable agricultural practices.

Control measures include reducing the use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides, promoting organic farming and integrated pest management, proper disposal of solid waste, recycling, banning harmful chemicals, and bioremediation (using microorganisms to break down pollutants).
The Soil Health Card Scheme (2015) gives farmers information on the nutrient status of their soil so they can use fertilizers correctly. Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in 2016.

sections.title: Noise Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Noise pollution is unwanted or excessive sound that disturbs normal activities and can harm health or well-being.

Noise pollution is unwanted or excessive sound that disturbs human beings and animals. Sound is measured in decibels (dB). Normal conversation is about 60 dB, while sounds above about 85 dB can damage hearing over long exposure.
In India, noise is regulated by the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

sections.title: Causes of Noise Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Traffic, construction, industries, generators, loudspeakers and other high-intensity sound sources are common causes.
Causes of noise pollution include vehicles and honking, aircraft, trains, industries, construction work, loudspeakers, firecrackers, generators and loud music at social and religious events.
In crowded urban areas such as Aizawl, heavy traffic on narrow roads is a major source of noise.

sections.title: Effects of Noise Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Excessive noise can cause stress, sleep disturbance, reduced concentration and hearing damage, especially with prolonged exposure.
Effects include hearing loss, stress, irritation, sleep disturbance, high blood pressure, headaches, lack of concentration and reduced work efficiency. Noise can also affect children's learning.
Noise disturbs wildlife, affecting their communication, breeding and migration.

sections.title: Control of Noise Pollution
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Controls include zoning, silencers and barriers, maintenance of machinery, regulation of loudspeakers and reduction of unnecessary noise at the source.

Control measures include regulating the use of loudspeakers and firecrackers, enforcing silence zones near hospitals, schools and courts, reducing unnecessary honking, maintaining vehicles, using sound barriers and green belts along roads, and soundproofing industries.

The Noise Rules, 2000, prescribe limits for different zones; for example, in residential areas the limit is 55 dB(A) during the day and 45 dB(A) at night, and in silence zones it is 50 dB(A) during the day and 40 dB(A) at night. Loudspeakers are generally not allowed between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., except in closed premises.

sections.title: Solid Waste
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Solid waste consists of discarded solid or semi-solid materials from households, institutions, commerce, industry and other activities.

Solid waste refers to unwanted or discarded solid materials from homes, businesses, industries, agriculture and institutions. It includes food waste, paper, plastics, glass, metals, construction debris, e-waste and hazardous waste.
Indian cities generate large amounts of municipal solid waste, and the amount is increasing with urbanization and changing lifestyles.

sections.title: Sources of Solid Waste
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Important sources include homes, markets, institutions, commercial establishments, industries, construction and certain agricultural activities.

Sources of solid waste include residential (households), commercial (shops, markets, hotels), institutional (schools, hospitals, offices), industrial, construction and demolition, agricultural and municipal services (street sweeping, parks).

Biomedical waste from hospitals and e-waste from discarded electronic devices require special handling. They are regulated by the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016, and the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022.

sections.title: Characteristics of Solid Waste
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Waste may differ in composition, moisture, density, biodegradability, combustibility and hazardous properties. These characteristics affect treatment and disposal.
Solid waste can be characterized by its physical properties (density, moisture content, particle size) and chemical properties (organic content, calorific value, presence of toxic substances).
In India, municipal solid waste usually has a high proportion of organic (biodegradable) material, which makes composting a suitable management method.

sections.title: Biodegradable Waste
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Biodegradable waste can be broken down by biological processes. Food waste and many plant materials are examples.
Biodegradable waste can be broken down by microorganisms into simpler substances. Examples include kitchen waste, vegetable peels, paper, garden waste and animal dung.
Biodegradable waste can be converted into compost or biogas, but if dumped in open areas it produces bad smells, attracts flies and rats, and releases methane, a greenhouse gas.

sections.title: Non-biodegradable Waste
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Non-biodegradable waste does not readily decompose biologically. Many plastics, metals and glass items fall into this broad category.
Non-biodegradable waste cannot be broken down easily by natural processes. Examples include plastics, glass, metals, rubber and certain chemicals.

Plastics can remain in the environment for hundreds of years and break down into microplastics that enter soil, water and food chains. India banned identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022 under the Plastic Waste Management Rules.

sections.title: Solid Waste Disposal
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Disposal is the final handling of waste after useful recovery and treatment. Sanitary landfilling is an engineered disposal method, unlike uncontrolled open dumping.
Methods of disposal include sanitary landfills, incineration, composting, recycling and waste-to-energy plants. Open dumping and open burning are harmful and should be avoided.
Disposal should be the last option after reducing, reusing and recycling waste.

sections.title: Solid Waste Management
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Solid waste management is the organised system of preventing, segregating, collecting, transporting, processing, recovering and safely disposing of solid waste.
Solid waste management involves the generation, segregation at source, storage, collection, transportation, processing (recycling, composting, energy recovery) and safe disposal of waste.

The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, require segregation of waste at source into biodegradable, non-biodegradable and domestic hazardous waste, and make waste generators responsible for segregation. The Swachh Bharat Mission (launched in 2014) promotes cleanliness and waste management.

sections.title: Waste Management Principles
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Important principles include preventing waste, reducing generation, segregating at source, recovering useful materials, treating suitable waste and safely disposing of residual waste.

The basic principles of waste management are the 3Rs (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle), often extended to 5Rs (Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle). The 'polluter pays' principle holds that those who cause pollution should bear the cost of managing it.
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) makes manufacturers responsible for collecting and recycling their products after use, and it applies in India to plastics, e-waste and batteries.

sections.title: Waste Hierarchy
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: The waste hierarchy gives preference to preventing and reducing waste, followed by reuse, recycling and recovery, while disposal is generally the least preferred option.

The waste hierarchy ranks waste management options from most preferred to least preferred: prevention (reducing waste at source), reuse, recycling, recovery (such as composting and energy recovery) and disposal (landfill).
The hierarchy is often shown as an inverted pyramid, with prevention at the top as the best option and disposal at the bottom as the last resort.

sections.title: Waste Segregation
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Segregation means separating different types of waste at the point of generation so that recyclable, biodegradable, hazardous and residual materials can be handled properly.

Waste segregation means separating waste into different categories at the source. In India, the common practice is to use green bins for wet (biodegradable) waste and blue bins for dry (non-biodegradable) waste, with separate handling for hazardous waste.
Segregation makes recycling and composting easier, reduces the amount of waste sent to landfills and protects waste workers from hazardous materials.

sections.title: Recycling
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Recycling processes discarded materials so that they can be used again as raw materials or products.
Recycling is the process of converting waste materials into new products. Common recyclable materials include paper, cardboard, glass, metals and some plastics.
Recycling saves raw materials and energy and reduces pollution. In India, the informal sector of waste pickers and scrap dealers (kabadiwalas) plays a major role in recycling.

sections.title: Composting
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Composting is controlled biological decomposition of suitable organic waste to produce a stable soil-like material.
Composting is the natural process of decomposing organic waste into a nutrient-rich material called compost, which improves soil fertility.
Vermicomposting uses earthworms to speed up composting. Households can compost kitchen waste in pits or bins, reducing waste and producing manure for gardens.

sections.title: Sanitary Landfill
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: A sanitary landfill is an engineered site designed to isolate residual waste and control environmental impacts more safely than open dumping.

A sanitary landfill is an engineered site where waste is spread in layers, compacted and covered with soil daily. It has a liner at the bottom to prevent leachate (polluted liquid from waste) from contaminating groundwater, and a system to collect methane gas.
Landfills require large areas of land and can cause problems if not properly managed, such as groundwater contamination, fires and bad smells.

sections.title: Incineration
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
SHORT NOTES

blocks.text: Incineration is controlled high-temperature combustion of suitable waste. It can reduce waste volume but requires proper emission control and is not appropriate for every waste stream.
Incineration is the burning of waste at high temperatures in a controlled facility. It reduces the volume of waste and can generate energy (waste-to-energy).

However, incineration can release harmful gases such as dioxins and furans if not properly controlled, and it is expensive. It is suitable mainly for non-recyclable combustible waste and biomedical waste.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT

sections.title: Environmental Pollution: Sources and Major Types
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Environmental pollution occurs when harmful substances or forms of energy cause undesirable changes in the environment. Pollution may arise from industries, transport, households, agriculture, construction, mining and waste disposal.

The VAC syllabus focuses on four major types: air, water, soil and noise pollution. Each has different sources and effects, but they can also be connected. For example, poorly managed waste may contaminate both soil and water, while burning waste can pollute air.

Pollution control therefore requires prevention at the source, proper treatment, regulation, responsible consumption and public participation. Understanding sources is important because effective control should prevent pollution before damage becomes severe.

Environmental pollution is the undesirable change in the characteristics of air, water or soil that harms living organisms. Pollutants may be primary or secondary, and biodegradable or non-biodegradable.

Sources of pollution include point sources (factories, sewage outlets) and non-point sources (agricultural runoff, vehicles). Major human sources are industries, transport, agriculture, mining, domestic waste and power generation.
The major types of pollution are air, water, soil and noise pollution, along with thermal, radioactive and light pollution.

India has enacted laws to control pollution, including the Water Act (1974), the Air Act (1981) and the Environment (Protection) Act (1986). The Central and State Pollution Control Boards enforce these laws, and the National Green Tribunal (established in 2010) hears environmental cases.
In conclusion, pollution control requires laws, technology, public awareness and individual responsibility.

sections.title: Air Pollution: Causes, Effects and Control
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Air pollution is the presence of harmful gases, particles or other contaminants in the atmosphere at damaging concentrations. Major human causes include vehicle emissions, industries, fossil-fuel burning, construction dust and open burning of waste.

Air pollution affects human health, especially the respiratory and cardiovascular systems. It can also reduce visibility, damage crops and vegetation and contribute to environmental problems beyond the immediate pollution source.

Control measures include cleaner energy, well-maintained vehicles, effective public transport, industrial emission-control equipment, dust management, enforcement of emission standards and avoidance of open burning.

The best approach combines technological control with reduced generation of pollutants.
Air pollution is the presence of harmful substances in the air. Major pollutants are particulate matter (PM10, PM2.5), sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, ozone and lead.
Causes include vehicle emissions, industries, thermal power plants, construction dust, crop residue burning, waste burning, domestic use of firewood and forest fires.

Effects include respiratory and heart diseases, lung cancer, acid rain, smog, ozone depletion and global warming. The Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) and the London smog (1952) are examples of air pollution disasters.

Control measures include cleaner fuels, Bharat Stage VI emission norms (2020), pollution control devices in industries, afforestation, public transport, electric vehicles, the National Clean Air Programme (2019) and the Air Act (1981).
In conclusion, clean air is essential for health, and both governments and citizens must act to reduce air pollution.

sections.title: Water Pollution: Causes, Effects and Control
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Water pollution occurs when contaminants change the quality of rivers, lakes, groundwater or other water bodies. Important causes include untreated sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, oil and improper disposal of solid waste.

Polluted water can transmit disease and may contain toxic chemicals. Nutrient pollution can promote excessive growth of algae and reduce dissolved oxygen, harming aquatic life. Pollutants can also move through food chains.

Control requires proper sewage treatment, industrial effluent treatment, responsible use of fertilisers and pesticides, protection of water bodies and prevention of waste dumping.

Safe water management is essential because water is both a human necessity and the foundation of aquatic ecosystems.
Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies, making water unsafe for drinking, agriculture and aquatic life. Water quality is measured by BOD, dissolved oxygen, pH and coliform bacteria.
Causes include untreated sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, oil spills, plastics and mining waste.
Effects include waterborne diseases (cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea), eutrophication, death of fish, biomagnification of toxins and diseases such as Minamata (mercury) and itai-itai (cadmium).

Control measures include sewage treatment, industrial effluent treatment, reducing chemical use in agriculture, banning dumping of waste, and programmes such as the Ganga Action Plan, Namami Gange and the Jal Jeevan Mission. The Water Act (1974) provides the legal framework.
In conclusion, clean water is a basic need, and protecting rivers, lakes and groundwater is a shared responsibility.

sections.title: Soil Pollution: Causes, Effects and Control
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Soil pollution occurs when harmful substances accumulate in soil or when waste disposal and chemical use degrade soil quality. Pesticides, excessive fertilisers, industrial wastes, mining residues, plastics and oil contamination are common causes.

Polluted soil may lose fertility and biological activity. Toxic substances can enter crops, groundwater and food chains, creating risks for ecosystems and human health.

Control measures include reducing unnecessary chemical inputs, treating industrial wastes, preventing uncontrolled dumping, recycling suitable materials and restoring contaminated sites.

Soil should be treated as a living environmental resource rather than simply as a place for waste disposal.
Soil pollution is the contamination of soil by harmful substances that reduce its fertility and harm living organisms.
Causes include excessive use of fertilizers and pesticides, industrial waste, mining, dumping of solid waste, e-waste, plastics and acid rain.
Effects include reduced crop yields, loss of soil organisms, contamination of food and groundwater, and health problems from heavy metals and pesticides.

Control measures include organic farming, integrated pest management, proper waste disposal, recycling, bioremediation, the Soil Health Card Scheme (2015) and stricter regulation of hazardous chemicals. Sikkim's success in becoming a fully organic state (2016) shows what is possible.
In conclusion, healthy soil is essential for food security, and its protection requires sustainable agricultural and waste management practices.

sections.title: Noise Pollution: Causes, Effects and Control
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Noise pollution is excessive or unwanted sound that interferes with normal life and can damage health. Traffic, construction, industrial machinery, generators and loudspeakers are common sources.

Long or intense exposure can contribute to hearing loss, stress, sleep disturbance and reduced concentration. Noise can also disturb animals and change their behaviour.

Control begins by reducing noise at its source. Proper maintenance, silencers, barriers, zoning and regulation of high-noise activities can help. Personal protection may be necessary in occupational environments.

Unlike many visible pollutants, noise leaves no physical residue, but its health and social effects can still be serious.
Noise pollution is unwanted or excessive sound measured in decibels (dB). Prolonged exposure to sound above about 85 dB can cause hearing damage.
Causes include traffic, honking, aircraft, industries, construction, loudspeakers, firecrackers and generators.
Effects include hearing loss, stress, sleep disturbance, high blood pressure, reduced concentration and disturbance to wildlife.

Control measures include enforcement of the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, silence zones near hospitals and schools, restrictions on loudspeakers and firecrackers at night, sound barriers and green belts, better vehicle maintenance and public awareness.
In conclusion, noise pollution is often ignored but has serious health effects, and simple individual actions such as avoiding unnecessary honking can help reduce it.

sections.title: Solid Waste: Sources, Characteristics and Disposal
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Solid waste is generated by households, markets, institutions, businesses, industries, construction and other activities. Its composition varies widely and may include organic matter, paper, plastic, glass, metal and other materials.

Important waste characteristics include biodegradability, moisture, density, combustibility and hazardous properties. These characteristics determine whether a material can be composted, recycled, treated or must be safely disposed of.

Uncontrolled dumping can cause odour, pests, fires, blocked drainage and contamination of soil and water. Open burning can also create air pollution.

Safe disposal should therefore occur only after waste prevention, recovery and treatment options have been considered. Residual waste may require engineered sanitary landfilling or another appropriate controlled method.

Solid waste is discarded solid material from households, commerce, industry, institutions, construction and agriculture. It includes biodegradable waste (food, paper, garden waste) and non-biodegradable waste (plastics, glass, metals).

Its characteristics depend on its source; Indian municipal waste generally has a high organic content. Special categories include biomedical waste, e-waste and hazardous waste, which need separate handling.
Disposal methods include sanitary landfills, incineration, composting and recycling. Open dumping and open burning are harmful because they pollute air, water and soil and spread disease.
Rules such as the Solid Waste Management Rules (2016), the Plastic Waste Management Rules (2016, with later amendments) and the E-Waste (Management) Rules (2022) regulate waste in India.
In conclusion, proper disposal is necessary, but reducing and recycling waste are better than disposal.

sections.title: Solid Waste Management: Principles, Hierarchy and Techniques
context: UNIT II — ENVIRONMENTAL POLLUTION AND WASTE MANAGEMENT
LONG NOTES

blocks.text:
Solid waste management covers the entire process from generation to final disposal. A good system begins with preventing unnecessary waste and segregating materials at the source.

The waste hierarchy ranks options according to preference. Prevention and reduction come first because the best waste is waste that is never created. Reuse extends the life of products. Recycling converts materials into new usable resources. Biological treatment such as composting is useful for suitable organic waste. Recovery and controlled treatment may be used for other fractions. Final disposal is reserved mainly for residual waste.

Techniques must match the characteristics of the waste. Composting is appropriate for segregated biodegradable material. Recycling requires clean recoverable materials. Incineration may be used for suitable waste under controlled conditions but requires emission management. Sanitary landfill is an engineered method for final residual disposal.

The key principle is that solid-waste management is not simply 'throwing waste away'. It is a planned system of prevention, segregation, recovery, treatment and safe disposal.

Solid waste management includes segregation, collection, transportation, processing and safe disposal of waste. Its principles are the 3Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle), the polluter pays principle and Extended Producer Responsibility.
The waste hierarchy ranks options from most to least preferred: prevention, reuse, recycling, recovery and disposal.
Techniques include segregation at source (green and blue bins), recycling, composting and vermicomposting, biogas production, sanitary landfills and incineration with energy recovery.

The Swachh Bharat Mission (2014) and the Solid Waste Management Rules (2016) emphasize segregation at source, door-to-door collection and community participation. In Mizoram, local councils, the YMA and municipal bodies organize cleanliness drives, and Aizawl is known for relatively clean streets and orderly traffic.
In conclusion, effective waste management requires government action, modern technology and, most importantly, responsible behaviour by every citizen.

sections.title: QUICK REVISION — VAC 103 IN ONE PAGE

blocks.text: Environmental Science = study of the environment and interactions among physical, biological and human components.
Natural resources = renewable and non-renewable resources that require responsible conservation.
Ecosystem = biotic components + abiotic components interacting as a functional unit.
Major ecosystems = terrestrial, aquatic and artificial.
Ecological succession = gradual change in a biological community over time.
Biodiversity = genetic diversity + species diversity + ecosystem diversity.
Biodiversity hotspot = exceptionally rich in endemic biodiversity and severely threatened by habitat loss.
Pollution syllabus = air + water + soil + noise.
For every pollution answer remember: Causes → Effects → Control.
Solid waste management = prevention → segregation → collection → recovery/treatment → safe disposal.
Waste hierarchy gives priority to prevention/reduction, then reuse and recycling/recovery; disposal is the last option.

Important laws and dates to remember: Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Water Act 1974, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Air Act 1981, Environment (Protection) Act 1986, Noise Rules 2000, Biological Diversity Act 2002, National Green Tribunal 2010, and Solid Waste Management Rules 2016.

Important international agreements: Ramsar Convention (1971), Montreal Protocol (1987), Rio Earth Summit and Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), Kyoto Protocol (1997) and Paris Agreement (2015).

For a 2–5 mark answer: define the term, write 3–5 clear points and add one example where useful. For a long answer on pollution, always organise it under Causes, Effects and Control. For an ecosystem answer, write Definition, Components, Structure and Functions. For biodiversity, distinguish genetic, species and ecosystem diversity. For solid waste management, explain the hierarchy in the correct direction and remember that open dumping and open burning are not proper management techniques.
Draw simple diagrams where they help: a food chain, a food web, an ecological pyramid, the stages of succession, or the waste hierarchy pyramid. Labelled diagrams often earn extra marks.

Including local examples from Mizoram, such as jhum cultivation, forest cover, the Indo-Burma hotspot, Dampa Tiger Reserve, bamboo flowering (mautam), or waste management in Aizawl, makes answers more relevant and interesting.
